history.heading: Kingdoms of the Congo Basin
paragraphs: The Democratic Republic of the Congo, Africa's second-largest country, covers most of the Congo River basin. The region was home to early hunter-gatherer peoples, and Bantu-speaking farmers spread through it over thousands of years. Powerful states arose, including the Kingdom of Kongo on the Atlantic coast, the Luba and Lunda empires in the south and the Kuba Kingdom, known for its art.
From the 16th century the Atlantic slave trade took large numbers of people from the region, and later Arab-Swahili traders raided the east for slaves and ivory.

history.heading: Congo Free State and Belgian Congo
paragraphs: At the 1884–85 Berlin Conference, King Leopold II of Belgium gained control of the territory as his personal property, the Congo Free State. To extract rubber and ivory, his regime used forced labour, hostage-taking and mutilation; millions of people died. International outrage forced Belgium to take over the colony in 1908.
The Belgian Congo became a major source of copper, diamonds and uranium, including the uranium used in the first atomic bombs. Very few Congolese received higher education under colonial rule.

history.heading: Independence and Mobutu
paragraphs: Congo became independent on 30 June 1960 with Patrice Lumumba as prime minister. The country quickly fell into crisis, with army mutinies and the secession of Katanga. Lumumba was overthrown and murdered in 1961 with Belgian and US involvement.
Joseph-Désiré Mobutu seized power in 1965, renamed the country Zaire in 1971 and ruled as a kleptocratic dictator for over three decades, supported by Western powers during the Cold War.

history.heading: The Congo wars and after
paragraphs: After the 1994 Rwandan genocide, conflict spilled into eastern Zaire. In 1997 rebels led by Laurent-Désiré Kabila and backed by Rwanda and Uganda overthrew Mobutu. A second war (1998–2003) drew in armies from nine African countries; together with the resulting disease and hunger, the conflicts caused millions of deaths.

Joseph Kabila succeeded his assassinated father in 2001. The 2018 election brought Félix Tshisekedi to power in the first peaceful transfer of power. Fighting in the east continued; in 2025 the M23 rebel group, backed by Rwanda, seized the cities of Goma and Bukavu, before US- and Qatar-brokered peace efforts.

culture.heading: Languages and peoples
paragraphs: The DRC has more than 200 ethnic groups. French is the official language and the DRC is the world's most populous French-speaking country, while Lingala, Swahili, Kikongo and Tshiluba are national languages. Most people are Christian, especially Catholic and Protestant, and the Kimbanguist Church is an indigenous Christian movement.

culture.heading: Music and arts
paragraphs: Congolese rumba, recognised by UNESCO, and its offshoot soukous have shaped popular music across Africa, with stars such as Franco, Papa Wemba and Koffi Olomide. Kinshasa, one of Africa's largest cities, has a vibrant arts and fashion scene, including the sapeurs.
Traditional sculpture and masks of the Kuba, Luba and Songye peoples are highly valued. Common foods include fufu, cassava leaves (pondu) and grilled fish.

politics.heading: Presidential republic
paragraphs: The DRC is a semi-presidential republic in which the president, elected for five years, holds strong powers, and a prime minister leads the government. Elections have been marred by logistical problems and disputes. Corruption and weak state institutions remain serious problems.

The east of the country, especially North and South Kivu and Ituri, has suffered decades of conflict involving over a hundred armed groups, with millions displaced. A UN peacekeeping mission has been present for over two decades.

economy.heading: Mineral wealth
paragraphs: The DRC has extraordinary mineral wealth. It produces around 70 percent of the world's cobalt, essential for batteries, and is a leading copper producer, along with diamonds, gold, tin and coltan. Mining in the southeast, much of it by Chinese companies, drives exports. Artisanal mining, sometimes involving child labour, is widespread.
The Congo River has enormous hydropower potential, and the country's rainforests are vital for the global climate.

economy.heading: Poverty
paragraphs: Despite its resources, the DRC is one of the poorest countries in the world, with most people living on very low incomes and relying on subsistence farming. Conflict, corruption, poor infrastructure and the illegal trade in minerals have prevented wealth from benefiting most people. The currency is the Congolese franc.
